title: Correlation, whether you meant to or not
lede: This page needs the smile vocabulary from page 07 and the variance machinery from page 11 — dispersion is almost always traded in variance rather than volatility, for reasons chapter 03 makes concrete.
claims: 39.5% against a 39.1% average implies correlation above one
curvature: index vol moves more per unit rho at 0.2 than at 0.6
correlation in the sell-off runs at 0.9 (realized so far rises past 0.6)

chapters.title: An index is not the average of its parts
chapters.dek: Twenty names averaging 39% volatility make an index of 9% or 39%, and the whole range is one parameter.

figures.title: Index volatility against correlation, with its ceiling and its floor
figures.caption: Notice the shape of the top curve: it rises steeply out of zero and then flattens. That curvature is why correlation is hard to trade — the same move in ρ is worth several times more index volatility at the bottom of the range than at the top, so a position that is comfortably sized at ρ = 0.6 is not comfortably sized at ρ = 0.2.

checks.q: Every stock in an index doubles its volatility overnight, and correlation is unchanged. What happens to index volatility?
checks.right: It exactly doubles. Every term in the double sum carries two volatility factors, so scaling all of them by two scales the variance by four and the volatility by two
checks.why: It exactly doubles. The formula is homogeneous of degree one in the volatilities — pull a common factor out of every σ and it comes straight through to σ_I. That is worth knowing precisely because it isolates what dispersion is really trading: not the level of volatility, which passes through untouched, but the correlation, which is the only thing left.

chapters.text: Take twenty stocks, equally weighted, with volatilities running from 22% to 56% — an average of 39.10% . What is the volatility of the index they form? The question has no answer until you say how they move together, and the range of possible answers is enormous. The algebra is a double sum. Index variance adds up every pair of names, each pair contributing its two weights, its two volatilities, and the correlation between them. The n terms where a name meets itself carry a correlation of one and cannot be diversified. The n²−n terms where two different names meet carry the correlation between them, and those are the terms that do all the work. Run the extremes. At ρ = 0 every cross term vanishes and only the diagonal survives, giving an index volatility of 9.05% — a fifth of the average name, purely from averaging away independent noise. At ρ = 1 every term survives at full weight and the index volatility is exactly 39.10% , the weighted average, which is also the mathematical ceiling. At a realistic ρ = 0.30 the index sits at 22.71% . So an index option is not a bet on its members' volatility. It is a bet on their volatility and on how much of it survives aggregation, and the second half is much larger than people expect. Between ρ = 0.15 and ρ = 0.50 — an unremarkable range — index volatility moves from 17.29% to 28.38%, with every single-name volatility held perfectly fixed. The lower panel checks that this is not just algebra. It simulates twenty genuinely correlated price paths, measures the realized volatility of the basket they produce, and compares it with the formula: 24.21% simulated against 24.25% predicted, a gap of four hundredths of a point. The identity is real, and it holds on paths rather than only on paper. [equation: σ_I² = Σ_i w_i²σ_i² + ρ · Σ_i≠j w_iw_jσ_iσ_j] Reads as: index variance is what each name contributes on its own, plus a correlation-weighted share of every pairing between different names. The first sum is small because the weights are squared; the second is large because there are so many pairs. Index volatility against correlation, with its ceiling and its floor Where index variance actually comes from The basket Notice the shape of the top curve: it rises steeply out of zero and then flattens. That curvature is why correlation is hard to trade — the same move in ρ is worth several times more index volatility at the bottom of the range than at the top, so a position that is comfortably sized at ρ = 0.6 is not comfortably sized at ρ = 0.2. The statistics underneath Two things moving together ↗ , in Chance, visually, builds correlation from paired draws. Try this Set correlation to exactly 1 and compare the index volatility with the average single-name volatility in the readout. Predict whether they are close or identical. Derivation — where the double sum comes from, and the one-number simplification The index return is the weighted sum of the component returns, so its variance is the variance of a sum. [equation: Var(Σ w_ir_i) = Σ_iΣ_j w_iw_j Cov(r_i, r_j)] Reads as: the variance of a portfolio is every pairwise covariance, weighted twice. Nothing here is specific to options; it is the same identity that produces portfolio theory. Write each covariance as ρ_ijσ_iσ_j and split the sum into the terms where i = j and the terms where it does not. [equation: σ_I² = Σ_i w_i²σ_i² + Σ_i≠j w_iw_jρ_ijσ_iσ_j] Reads as: the diagonal is undiversifiable and the off-diagonal is where correlation lives. With n names there are n diagonal terms and n²−n off-diagonal ones, so for any decent-sized index the second sum dominates. Everything on this page then replaces the whole correlation matrix with a single average ρ . That is a real simplification and it is the one the market makes too, because a single number is what can be quoted and hedged. Where it breaks. One ρ cannot describe a market where sectors move together and against each other, and the failure is not symmetric: a basket with two tightly correlated blocks has the same average pairwise correlation as one that is uniformly loosely correlated, and behaves nothing like it in a stress. Dispersion books hedged on average correlation carry exactly this exposure, and it shows up as an unexplained residual in precisely the moves that matter. The second simplification is weights: index weights drift with prices, so a basket matched today is not matched in three months.

chapters.title: Nobody quotes correlation, so you invert for it
chapters.dek: Take the index price, take the component prices, and solve the formula backwards. What comes out is a number with opinions baked into it.

figures.title: Quoted index volatility mapped to implied correlation
figures.caption: Push the quoted index volatility toward the weighted average of the components and watch implied correlation run into its ceiling. Everything to the right of that vermilion line is not an expensive index, it is an inconsistent set of prices — and the check for it costs one line of arithmetic.

checks.q: Two desks report implied correlation on the same index on the same day: 0.38 and 0.51. Who is wrong?
checks.right: Possibly neither. The inversion depends on expiry, on whether you use at-the-money or variance strikes, and on how many components you include; different recipes give different answers from identical prices
checks.why: Possibly neither. Implied correlation is a derived quantity, not an observed one, and the derivation has at least three free choices in it. The practical rule is that a correlation number is only comparable with another number built the same way — which is why desks track their own series rather than a published one, and why cross-desk arguments about "the level of correlation" are usually arguments about methodology.

terms.Implied correlation: The single average correlation that makes the index formula reproduce the quoted index volatility. Inferred rather than observed, so it inherits every choice made in the inversion.

chapters.text: There is no correlation screen. What exists is an index option market and twenty single-name option markets, and the bridge between them is chapter 01's identity read from right to left. Fix every σ_i at its implied volatility, fix σ_I at the index's implied volatility, and there is exactly one ρ that makes the equation true. That number is implied correlation , and it is the closest thing the market has to a price for co-movement. The mapping is steep, which is the first practical thing to know. On our basket, an index quoted at 20% implies 0.220 ; at 25% it implies 0.375 ; at 28% it implies 0.485 . Three volatility points of index move a correlation estimate by more than a tenth, so a stale index mark or a mismatched snapshot time produces a correlation number that is badly wrong while looking perfectly plausible. The second thing to know is that the inversion inherits every choice you made on the way in. Which expiry? Which strike — at-the-money volatility, or the variance strike from page 11 , which carries a skew premium? Do you use all five hundred names or the top fifty as a proxy? Each answer produces a different implied correlation from the same market, and they do not agree to two decimal places. A quoted implied correlation without its recipe is not a number. The lower panel splits index variance into the part that survives no matter what — the diagonal — and the part that correlation controls. On a twenty-name basket the diagonal is small: at ρ = 0.3 it supplies about a tenth of index variance, and the rest is the correlation term. That is the mechanical reason index volatility is so sensitive to a parameter nobody observes. [equation: ρ_imp = (σ_I² − Σ w_i²σ_i²) / Σ_i≠j w_iw_jσ_iσ_j] Reads as: take the index variance, remove the part that cannot be diversified, and express what is left as a fraction of the most it could possibly be. That fraction is the implied correlation. Quoted index volatility mapped to implied correlation Index variance split into its two sources Today's marks Push the quoted index volatility toward the weighted average of the components and watch implied correlation run into its ceiling. Everything to the right of that vermilion line is not an expensive index, it is an inconsistent set of prices — and the check for it costs one line of arithmetic. chapters.title: The trade, and what it is actually long
chapters.dek: Sell index variance, buy the components' variance, and the volatility level cancels. What is left is a straight line in realized correlation.

figures.title: Dispersion P&L against realized correlation
figures.caption: The lower panel is the control experiment and it is the point of the chapter. Multiply every single-name volatility by any factor you like with realized correlation at the level you sold, and the net line sits on zero at every multiplier — both legs scale together. Move realized correlation away and the multiplier scales the correlation P&L by its square, which is why the same correlation miss costs far more in a violent market. The position is genuinely insensitive to the thing everybody talks about and completely exposed to the thing nobody quotes.

figures.title: Run a dispersion book
figures.caption: Sold at 0.5, the book makes $607,000 over forty calm days in which stocks move on their own news. Then a twelve-day sell-off drives correlation to 0.9, everything falls together, and $455,000 of it is gone; the book ends the quarter $172,000 up. Sold at 0.4, close to what the calm market delivers, it makes $93,000 before the sell-off and finishes $638,000 down. The premium in implied correlation is what pays for the days it goes to one.

checks.q: You are short index variance and long component variance. The market crashes: every single-name volatility triples. What happened to your P&L?
checks.right: It depends almost entirely on correlation, and in a crash correlation rises too. The volatility level cancels between the legs; the correlation move does not, and it goes against you
checks.why: Correlation decides it, and in a crash correlation is the thing that moves against you. The first answer is the seductive one because being long twenty variance swaps into a crash sounds wonderful, and it would be — except that you are short the index's variance in matched size, and the index's variance rises by more than the components' when everything moves together. Chapter 05 puts numbers on how much more.

chapters.text: Dispersion is the trade that expresses chapter 01 directly. Sell variance on the index, buy variance on each of its members in matched size, and hold both to expiry. If the names move around a lot but independently, the components pay and the index does not, and you win. If everything moves together, the index pays more than the components and you lose. The reason it is traded in variance rather than volatility is chapter 01's identity, which is exactly linear in variance and a mess in volatility. Buy each component's variance in proportion to its index weight, scaled so the long leg's total variance equals the index's at the correlation you sold, and the position's P&L reduces to the difference between implied and realized correlation, multiplied by the size of the off-diagonal sum. That is a clean exposure. Try the same thing with volatility swaps or straddles and the relationship is approximate and drifts with spot. The figure runs it. With implied correlation at 0.35 — an index implied of 24.25% against those components — the P&L line crosses zero at realized correlation of exactly 0.35 and is a straight line either side. Realized correlation of 0.15 and the short index leg wins comfortably; realized 0.60 and it loses a quarter more than it made in the good case — 0.25 of correlation against 0.20, on a straight line — and the line keeps going. Three practical things the figure cannot show. Trading twenty single-name variance swaps means twenty bid–offers against one, so the entry cost is asymmetric and the trade needs a decent gap between implied and expected realized just to break even. Weights drift, so a matched basket stops being matched. And the components have their own wing problems from page 11 chapter 04 — single-name variance is exactly the product whose replication is most fragile, and you are long twenty of them. [equation: P&L ∝ (ρ_imp − ρ_realized) · Σ_i≠j w_iw_jσ_iσ_j] Reads as: you are paid the difference between the correlation you sold and the correlation that happened, scaled by how much correlation there was to sell. Nothing about the level of volatility survives into this expression. Then a twelve-day sell-off drives correlation to 0.9, everything falls together, and $455,000 of it is gone; the book ends the quarter $172,000 up. Sold at 0.4, close to what the calm market delivers, it makes $93,000 before the sell-off and finishes $638,000 down. The premium in implied correlation is what pays for the days it goes to one. Trader's lens A dispersion trader is short correlation and knows exactly when it will hurt: in a sell-off, when every stock becomes the same trade. The edge is that index options are persistently expensive relative to their parts, because everyone who needs portfolio insurance buys the index. The risk is that the insurance is needed, all at once. Sell correlation only at a level that has already paid for the last crash. Weight the long legs carefully: vega-neutral, theta-neutral and correlation-neutral are three different books (chapter 06). The worst days for dispersion are the best days for the people who bought index puts from you. Rule of thumb: the book's daily edge is roughly proportional to implied minus realized correlation, times the variance of the stocks.

chapters.title: Why implied correlation is persistently rich
chapters.dek: Two large, opposite, structural flows push on the two legs. The gap between them is the trade's carry, and also the reason it is crowded.

figures.title: Two flows, one residual
figures.caption: Neither slider expresses a view about correlation, and both move implied correlation. That is the whole mechanism: correlation is inferred from two prices that are each being pushed around by unrelated demand, so it records the flow imbalance rather than anybody's forecast.

checks.q: A large bank stops issuing autocallables , cutting the supply of single-name volatility. All else equal, what happens to implied correlation?
checks.right: It falls. Less single-name selling lifts component implied volatility, and with index implied unchanged the inversion returns a lower correlation
checks.why: It falls. Implied correlation is the residual that reconciles two option markets, so anything that moves either market moves it — including events with no informational content about how stocks co-move at all. This is why the number is better read as a flow indicator than as a forecast, and why "correlation is cheap" is often a statement about issuance calendars.

terms.Autocallables: Structured notes that pay a coupon and redeem early if the underlying stays above a barrier. The investor is short a down-and-in put, so issuing them leaves the bank long single-name volatility, which it sells into the market — one half of the flow story.

chapters.text: Implied correlation has historically sat above subsequently realized correlation more often than not. That is a claim about a persistent premium, and a persistent premium needs a persistent reason, not a story about sentiment. The reason here is flow, and it is the same argument page 09's bridge chapter makes about the surface generally: durable one-way demand shows up as a price. The two flows push in opposite directions on the two legs of the same trade. Index volatility is bid. Institutions hedging equity portfolios buy index puts, because one index hedge is cheaper and simpler to administer than five hundred single-name hedges, and because a mandate usually specifies portfolio-level protection. That demand is structural, price-insensitive within limits, and one-directional. It lifts index implied volatility. Single-name volatility is offered. Overwriting programs, structured-product issuance and yield-enhancement mandates all sell single-name volatility — calls in the first case, mostly downside puts embedded in notes in the second. That supply is also structural and one-directional, and it depresses single-name implied volatility. Now put them into chapter 02's inversion. Index implied up, component implied down, and the implied correlation that reconciles them must rise — even if nobody involved held any opinion about correlation at all. The number is a residual, and residuals absorb whatever the flows do to the inputs. Two honest qualifications, because this is exactly the kind of claim that gets stated too confidently. The premium is not a free lunch: it is compensation for taking the other side of a hedge that pays off in crashes, and chapter 05 is what you are being paid for. And it is not constant — the flows change with issuance cycles and with how much index hedging is fashionable, so a strategy calibrated to one regime's premium can find it has gone. Two flows, one residual Flow pressure Neither slider expresses a view about correlation, and both move implied correlation. That is the whole mechanism: correlation is inferred from two prices that are each being pushed around by unrelated demand, so it records the flow imbalance rather than anybody's forecast.

chapters.title: Correlation goes to one exactly when you need it not to
chapters.dek: The variable is bounded above, the position is short it, and the bound is reached in the one scenario the position was never sized for.

figures.title: Calm, correlation stress, and full stress
figures.caption: Drag correlation and the volatility multiplier together, the way a real crash moves them, and watch the two legs stop offsetting. The gap between the vermilion and moss lines in the lower panel is the loss, and it opens fastest in the top-right corner — which is the only corner that matters.

checks.q: Why is a dispersion book's worst day usually also the firm's worst day?
checks.right: Because it is short correlation, and correlation spikes in exactly the broad sell-offs that hurt every other long-biased book at the same time. The diversification you thought you had is the thing that fails
checks.why: It is short the thing that defines a crash. A crash is a correlation event — that is close to what the word means at portfolio level. So a short-correlation position is not merely unlucky in those episodes, it is structurally aligned with them, and its returns look wonderful right up until the day they explain themselves. Sizing it as though its historical volatility described its risk is the specific mistake.

chapters.text: Every risk on this page collapses into a single sentence. A dispersion position is short correlation; correlation has a hard ceiling at one; and markets travel toward that ceiling in exactly the episodes where everything else is going wrong too. The trade's worst case is not a tail of a smooth distribution — it is a regime change, and it arrives with the rest of the portfolio's worst case. Put numbers on it with our basket. In a calm market at ρ = 0.25 , index volatility is 21.06% . Move correlation alone to 0.90 , touching no single-name volatility at all, and index volatility goes to 37.20% — a rise of 16.14 points produced entirely by co-movement. Now do what actually happens and let single-name volatilities rise as well, say by 1.8× : index volatility reaches 66.97% , up 45.91 points from calm. Watch what that does to the two legs. Measured from the 0.35 correlation the trade was sold at, the short index variance leg loses 3,896 variance units. The long component leg, sized to be variance-neutral at inception and supposed to be the hedge, gains only 1,318 . Net, the book is down 2,579 — and every unit of that is the correlation move, magnified by the square of the volatility multiplier. The trade is not volatility-neutral in a crash because it was never a volatility trade — the legs only cancel while correlation is where you left it. Two more failure modes worth naming, both of which turn a bad outcome into an unmanageable one. The average is not the matrix. A single ρ cannot distinguish a market that has become uniformly more correlated from one that has split into two blocks. Books hedged on average correlation carry the difference as an unhedged residual, and it is largest in stress, when the correlation structure is changing shape rather than just level. Liquidity leaves both legs at once. Single-name variance is the product from page 11 chapter 07 whose replication depends on a put wing that gaps and widens in a crash. Twenty of those, against one index position, is a lot of fragility concentrated in one direction. And the arithmetic check from chapter 02 becomes a live risk control here. Because index volatility can never exceed the weighted average of its components, an index quoted at 39.5% against components averaging 39.10% implies a correlation of 1.0217 — which is impossible, and therefore evidence that a mark is stale, a proxy basket is wrong, or something is genuinely dislocated. It is one line of arithmetic and it is worth running every day. [equation: σ_I ≤ Σ_i w_iσ_i always] Reads as: an index can never be more volatile than the weighted average of its members. Equality needs perfect correlation, so a quote above that line is not a price, it is a broken input. chapters.title: How big the long leg is decides what else you own
chapters.dek: Every dispersion book has to choose how much single-name variance to buy against the index. The two common answers leave different bets behind.

figures.title: P&L when every volatility moves by the same factor
figures.caption: With realized correlation equal to implied, the blue line lies on zero: the theta-weighted book is a correlation trade and nothing else. The red line is that same trade plus a long position in the level of volatility.

checks.q: You want a dispersion book whose only exposure is realized against implied correlation. Which sizing?
checks.right: Theta-weighted, since it matches the variance the two legs are paid on
checks.why: Theta-weighted. The correlation exposure is the same either way, which is why the last answer is tempting, but the question asked for the only exposure. Vega-weighting adds a long-vol position, and equal notional adds a much larger one.

chapters.text: Short $1,000 per point squared of index variance at the 24.25 implied from chapter 03, long the twenty names in equal weights. The figure scales every single-name volatility by the same factor, holds realized correlation where you set it, and shows each sizing's P&L. P&L when every volatility moves by the same factor The market With realized correlation equal to implied, the blue line lies on zero: the theta-weighted book is a correlation trade and nothing else. The red line is that same trade plus a long position in the level of volatility. Theta-weighted sizes the single-name leg so its implied variance equals the index's: 0.359 of a unit of each name per unit of index. If every name realizes its implied, both legs pay the same, and if every vol rises by the same proportion the two legs still move together. What is left is the correlation bet and nothing else, which is the sizing chapter 03 used. Vega-weighted sizes it so the vega on each side matches: 0.620. That is 73% more single-name variance, and the extra is a naked long-vol position. If every vol rises by 80% with correlation unchanged it makes $956,000 ; if every vol falls 40% it loses $273,000 . Matching vega does not make a dispersion book vol-neutral, because an index vol point and a single-name vol point are different sizes of move. Neither sizing changes the correlation bet. Realized correlation at 0.60 instead of 0.35, vols unchanged, costs both books the same $362,000 , because correlation lives only in the index leg. The choice decides what you hold alongside it. In the crisis case from chapter 05, every vol up 80% and correlation at 0.90, the theta-weighted book loses $2.58 million and the vega-weighted book $1.62 million : the long-vol tilt cushions exactly the scenario that hurts dispersion most, and pays for it by losing whenever vols drift lower. [equation: theta-weighted k = σ_I² ÷ Σ w_iσ_i² vega-weighted k = σ_I ÷ Σ w_iσ_i] Reads as: theta-weighting matches the variance on each side; vega-weighting matches the volatility. Because the index vol is below the average name vol, the second number is always the larger, and the difference is a long position in vol. Try this Set realized correlation to 0.90. Predict whether the two lines cross anywhere.

chapters.title: Check yourself

checks.q: Twenty names average 39% volatility. What is the highest the index volatility can possibly be?
checks.right: Exactly 39%. Correlation of one gives the weighted average and there is nothing above that
checks.why: The weighted average is a hard ceiling. It is also a live arbitrage check — an index quoted above it implies correlation above one, which means an input is broken.

checks.q: The same twenty names, but correlation is zero. Roughly what is the index volatility?
checks.right: About 9%. The diagonal terms survive, so idiosyncratic variance leaves a floor that diversification cannot remove
checks.why: About 9%. Independence removes the cross terms, not the individual variances. With equal weights that floor falls like one over the square root of the number of names, which is why it is small but never zero.

checks.q: Why is implied correlation so sensitive to the index mark?
checks.right: Because the diagonal term is small, so almost all of index variance is the correlation term — three points of index volatility can move implied correlation by more than a tenth
checks.why: The correlation term carries almost all of index variance. A small residual computed as a difference between two large-ish numbers amplifies any error in either, so stale or mistimed marks produce plausible-looking nonsense.

checks.q: Why is dispersion traded in variance rather than volatility?
checks.right: Because the index identity is exactly linear in variance. Match variance notionals and the P&L is a clean straight line in realized correlation; match anything else and it is approximate and drifts
checks.why: The algebra is linear in variance and not in volatility. This is the practical reason page 11 comes before this one — dispersion is the clearest application of why the square is the tradeable object.

checks.q: What makes implied correlation persistently rich?
checks.right: Two opposite structural flows: index hedging bids index volatility while overwriting and structured-product issuance offer single-name volatility. Correlation is the residual that reconciles them
checks.why: Flow on both legs, pushing the same way. Neither side of that flow has any opinion about correlation, which is the point — the number records a supply-and-demand imbalance in two separate markets, and it is compensation for taking the other side of a crash hedge.

checks.q: Correlation moves from 0.25 to 0.90 with every single-name volatility unchanged. What happens to index volatility on our basket?
checks.right: It rises from about 21% to about 37% — sixteen points, produced entirely by co-movement
checks.why: 21% to 37%, from correlation alone. This is the single most useful number on the page for sizing: it is what a short-correlation position loses before any volatility has moved at all, and it is why historical P&L volatility badly understates the risk.
